slots.practicalActivity: Open Task Manager (Windows), Activity Monitor (Mac), or run top and ps aux on a Linux machine/WSL. Identify your machine's CPU, RAM, and storage usage, then find the single process using the most CPU and the one using the most memory, noting each one's PID. Write one sentence connecting what you see to each of the OS's three jobs from the lesson: process scheduling, memory management, and device/file access.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of your process list with the top CPU and top memory consumer circled or noted, plus 3 written sentences mapping what you observed to scheduling, memory management, and device/file access.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Oracle VirtualBox (a Type 2 hypervisor) or enable WSL2, and create one virtual machine or WSL instance. On your host machine, start a simple local web server (e.g. `python -m http.server 8000`) so the host is acting as a server; from inside the VM, open a browser and request a page from the host's IP address, making the VM the client in that exchange. Note which machine initiated the request and which one answered.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot showing a successful request from the VM to the host's local web server, plus a one-sentence note identifying which machine was the client and which was the server in that exchange.

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /all (Windows) or ip addr / ifconfig (Mac/Linux) on your own machine and identify your IP address, your network's LAN scope, and your default gateway. Then build a 4-row table mapping 4 different hypothetical connection failures (no link light on a cable; local devices unreachable; local traffic works but nothing beyond the router does; the server responds but the application times out) to the correct OSI/TCP-IP layer and which device you'd check first for each.
slots.deliverable: Your own machine's IP configuration output, plus a written 4-row table mapping 4 failure symptoms to the correct network layer and the device to check.

slots.practicalActivity: Find your machine's private IP address (ipconfig / ifconfig) and your public IP address (search "what is my IP"), and write down why they're different. Then classify this list of 8 addresses as public or private, citing the specific reserved range for each private one: 10.4.2.1, 203.0.113.9, 192.168.50.7, 8.8.8.8, 172.20.0.5, 198.51.100.23, 192.168.1.1, 172.40.0.9 (note: the last one is NOT in the private range even though it looks similar — explain why).
slots.deliverable: Your own private and public IP addresses with a one-sentence explanation of the difference, plus a completed public/private classification of all 8 listed addresses with the reserved range cited for each private one.

slots.practicalActivity: By hand (no subnet calculator), work out the usable host count for /24, /25, /26, /27, and /28, showing the 2^n - 2 math for each. Then design a subnet plan for a fictional branch office with 45 devices today and room to grow to 60: pick the tightest-fitting CIDR, and write out the network address, the full usable host range, and the broadcast address, starting from 192.168.20.0.
slots.deliverable: A written table of usable hosts for /24 through /28 with the math shown, plus a complete subnet plan (CIDR, network address, usable range, broadcast address) sized correctly for 45-60 devices.

slots.practicalActivity: On your own machine, run arp -a to see the MAC-to-IP mappings your machine has learned on its local subnet (the same job a switch's MAC address table does), then run ip route (Linux/WSL) or netstat -r / route print (Mac/Windows) to view your own routing table and identify your default gateway. Write a 4-step walkthrough, in your own words, of what happens when your machine sends a packet to an address outside your subnet, using the lesson's step-by-step decision process.
slots.deliverable: Your machine's ARP table and routing table output with the default gateway identified, plus a written 4-step walkthrough of how a packet leaving your subnet gets forwarded.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending subnetting drill for Networking Foundations: design complete subnet plans for 3 different device counts — 12 devices, 50 devices, and 200 devices — choosing the tightest-fitting CIDR for each and showing the network address, usable range, and broadcast address for every plan, the same way the lesson sized the Northbridge Retail warehouse subnet.
slots.deliverable: 3 fully worked subnet plans (one each for 12, 50, and 200 devices), each showing CIDR, network address, usable host range, and broadcast address.

slots.practicalActivity: Install dig (or use nslookup on Windows) and run it against 3 real domains, capturing the A record, its TTL, and at least one MX or TXT record for one of them. Then write a short scenario explaining what would happen, and for how long, if one of those domains migrated to a new server and its TTL was 3600 seconds but nobody lowered it beforehand.
slots.deliverable: dig/nslookup output for 3 real domains showing at least an A record and TTL for each, plus a short written explanation of the stale-DNS risk for an un-lowered TTL before a migration.

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /all (Windows) or check your network settings (Mac/Linux) to find your own DHCP lease details: the assigned IP, the DHCP server address, and the lease obtained/expiration times. Then write out the 4-step DORA exchange (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) narrated specifically for your own device joining your home or office network this morning.
slots.deliverable: Your own machine's real DHCP lease details (IP, DHCP server, lease times), plus a written DORA walkthrough narrated for your own device.

slots.practicalActivity: For 5 real applications or scenarios you choose yourself (e.g. a video call, an online banking login, a multiplayer game's position updates, a file download, a live stock ticker), decide whether TCP or UDP fits each one and justify it in one sentence citing the specific tradeoff (reliability/ordering vs. speed). Then run curl -v against a real HTTPS site and point out, from the connection log, where TCP's handshake had to complete before any HTTP data moved.
slots.deliverable: A 5-row table assigning TCP or UDP to 5 real applications with a one-sentence justification each, plus curl -v output with the TCP handshake portion identified.

slots.practicalActivity: Run curl -v against 3 real HTTPS sites and record each one's status code, at least 2 response headers, and the TLS handshake lines showing the certificate exchange. In your browser, click the padlock icon on one of those sites and inspect its certificate's subject, issuer (Certificate Authority), and expiration date, matching each field to what the lesson said a certificate actually contains.
slots.deliverable: curl -v output for 3 real HTTPS sites with status codes, headers, and TLS handshake lines captured, plus a certificate inspection (subject, issuer, expiration) for one of them from the browser's padlock view.

slots.practicalActivity: Open your OS's built-in firewall (Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security, or macOS's Firewall under Security & Privacy) and inspect its current inbound rules. Add one new inbound rule that allows TCP traffic only on a specific port (e.g. 8000, to match a local test server) from your own local network, then write out that rule's 5 fields (direction, protocol, port, source, action) exactly as the lesson's rule-building table shows them, and explain in one sentence why "default deny" is the safer starting posture.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of one real inbound firewall rule you created on your own machine, its 5 fields written out in the lesson's table format, and a one-sentence explanation of default deny.

slots.practicalActivity: Compare your machine's private IP (ipconfig/ifconfig) against your public IP ("what is my IP") again, but this time explain specifically how NAT is the mechanism bridging the two every time you reach the internet. Then log into your home router's admin page (usually 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1) and locate its port forwarding settings screen — without necessarily changing anything live, write down exactly what external port, internal IP, internal port, and protocol you would configure to forward a local web server on port 8000 to be reachable from outside.
slots.deliverable: A written explanation of how NAT translates your traffic using your own real private/public IP pair, plus a filled-out port forwarding configuration (external port, internal IP, internal port, protocol) for a hypothetical local service.

slots.practicalActivity: Start two simple local web servers on different ports (e.g. python -m http.server 8001 and 8002, each serving a different one-line index.html so you can tell them apart), install Nginx locally, and configure it as a reverse proxy/load balancer in front of both using the round-robin algorithm. Send 6 repeated curl requests to Nginx's address and confirm the responses alternate between your two backend servers.
slots.deliverable: An Nginx config file set up as a round-robin reverse proxy over 2 local backend servers, plus curl output from at least 6 requests showing traffic alternating between both backends.

slots.practicalActivity: Research 2 real VPN products or features — one built for site-to-site connections (e.g. an AWS Site-to-Site VPN or Azure VPN Gateway) and one built for remote-access (e.g. WireGuard or a commercial remote-access VPN client) — and write a comparison table matching each to the lesson's site-to-site vs. remote-access distinction. Then design, on paper, a bastion host setup for a fictional 3-server private subnet: name which single server is the bastion, and write the one firewall rule each of the other 3 servers would need (allowing SSH only from the bastion's address).
slots.deliverable: A written comparison table of a real site-to-site VPN product and a real remote-access VPN product, plus a bastion host design showing one hardened entry point and the restrictive firewall rule for each of 3 protected servers.

slots.practicalActivity: Run ping, traceroute (tracert on Windows), and dig against 3 real domains of your choice. For each domain, record the ping round-trip time, the number of hops traceroute reports, and the IP address dig resolves the name to. Then write 2-3 sentences explaining, using this lesson's "use them together" order, how you'd apply these three tools in sequence if a teammate reported one of those sites as "not loading."
slots.deliverable: ping, traceroute, and dig output for 3 real domains, plus a written explanation of the correct order to run these three tools when diagnosing a "site is down" report.

slots.practicalActivity: Run curl -v against 3 real URLs and record the status code each one returns (aim for at least one 200 and, if possible, one 404 by requesting a path you know doesn't exist). On your own machine, run ss -tuln (Linux/WSL) or netstat -an (Windows/Mac) and identify at least 3 ports your machine is actually listening on, naming which application you believe owns each one.
slots.deliverable: curl -v output for 3 URLs with status codes recorded, plus ss/netstat output identifying at least 3 locally listening ports and the likely application behind each.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out a full bottom-up troubleshooting walkthrough (reachability, DNS, transport, application) for this fictional ticket: "Some customers say checkout.northbridgeretail.com is down, but our monitoring dashboard says it's fine." At each of the 4 steps, name the specific tool you'd run and what result would let you rule that layer out versus confirm it as the problem, then write one falsifiable hypothesis (not a vague guess) for what the actual cause might be.
slots.deliverable: A written 4-step bottom-up troubleshooting plan for the given ticket, naming the tool and expected result at each layer, plus one specific, falsifiable hypothesis for the root cause.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick 2 of the lesson's 4 failure scenarios (stale DNS, expired certificate, misconfigured firewall, overloaded backend) and find a real-world piece of evidence for each using actual tools: check a real site's certificate expiration date in your browser's padlock view, or run dig against a domain from two different DNS resolvers (e.g. 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1) to see if they ever disagree. Write down which first clue (from the lesson's table) would tip you off to each scenario in a real incident.
slots.deliverable: Real evidence gathered for 2 of the 4 failure scenarios (a certificate expiration check and/or a dig comparison across two resolvers), with the matching first-clue signal written out for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending troubleshooting lab for Troubleshooting: given this fictional symptom — "api.northbridgeretail.com pings fine but every request to it times out" — run the actual bottom-up methodology with real commands against a real site you pick to practice the motions (dig, ping, curl -v, and ss/netstat on your own machine), writing down what each command's real output would mean at each stage if it mapped to this exact symptom.
slots.deliverable: A written, command-by-command troubleshooting trace (dig, ping, curl -v, ss/netstat) against a real site, each step annotated with what that result would mean for the "pings fine, every request times out" symptom.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free-tier account on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud (no need to launch anything paid) and browse its console's service catalog. Find and name one real service that's IaaS (a raw virtual machine product), one that's PaaS (a managed app-hosting product), and one that's SaaS-like (a fully managed end-user product), writing one sentence for each explaining which layer you manage versus which the provider manages.
slots.deliverable: Names of 3 real services from one cloud provider's console — one IaaS, one PaaS, one SaaS-like — each with a one-sentence explanation of the management split.

slots.practicalActivity: In your cloud provider's console (no resources need to actually launch), browse the list of available regions and, for one region, the list of availability zones inside it. Design, on paper, a resiliency plan for a fictional retail checkout service: which region you'd deploy to first (justify by proximity to your own location), how many availability zones you'd spread it across and why, and whether you'd also set up a region pair, citing the specific risk each choice protects against.
slots.deliverable: A written resiliency plan naming a real region and its availability zones from your cloud console, with justified choices for zone spread and whether a region pair is warranted.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a 3-column table (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) with these 6 rows: physical data center security, hypervisor patching, OS patching, application code, data classification, user access control. Mark each cell "Provider" or "Customer" based on the service model, matching the lesson's shifting line. Then write 2-3 sentences explaining, with a concrete example, why "the cloud got hacked" is almost always actually a customer-side misconfiguration rather than a provider failure.
slots.deliverable: A completed 6-row by 3-column shared-responsibility table (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), plus a short written explanation of why most real cloud breaches are customer misconfigurations.

slots.practicalActivity: Open the Azure Pricing Calculator (or the AWS or GCP equivalent) and build a real cost estimate for a small setup: one small VM running continuously, 50 GB of storage, and an estimated amount of monthly data egress. Try the estimate twice — once as pay-as-you-go and once with reserved pricing if available — and note the dollar difference. Add 2 tags to the estimate (e.g. team: checkout, environment: production) and explain in one sentence why tagging matters once a bill covers dozens of resources.
slots.deliverable: A real pricing-calculator estimate (screenshot or exported summary) comparing pay-as-you-go vs. reserved pricing for the same small setup, with 2 tags applied and a one-sentence note on why tagging matters.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Design and Troubleshoot a Small Network

slots.practicalActivity: Design, on paper, the full addressing and connectivity plan for the capstone's regional distribution office brief: a subnet sized for ~50 devices with its network/usable range/broadcast address (using your Chapter 2 subnetting skills), a note on which devices get DHCP vs. a static reservation, a firewall rule set naming only the ports the office actually needs open, and a decision on site-to-site vs. remote-access VPN for reaching the cloud-hosted inventory system.
slots.deliverable: A written network design document covering the subnet plan, DHCP/static address assignments, a firewall rule list, and a justified VPN connectivity choice for the 50-device office brief.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply the identify-isolate-test-resolve methodology in writing to the capstone's broken scenario: the cloud inventory system times out from the new office even though "the VPN is up." Document each step with a specific command you'd run (e.g. ping the VPN gateway itself vs. ping the inventory system's address) and what result at each step rules something in or out, arriving at the same root cause the lesson describes — an outbound firewall rule that was never updated for the inventory system's IP range.
slots.deliverable: A written identify/isolate/test/resolve trace for the broken VPN-adjacent connectivity scenario, with a specific command and expected result at each of the 4 steps, ending in the correct root cause and fix.

slots.practicalActivity: Continue the capstone build: draw a simple architecture diagram (even hand-drawn or built in a free tool like draw.io) showing the office subnet, the firewall, the VPN tunnel, and the cloud-hosted systems it connects to. Write the actual firewall rule set (direction/protocol/port/source/action for each rule) that implements your Chapter 4 security design, including the specific missing rule your Chapter 5-style troubleshooting identified.
slots.deliverable: An architecture diagram showing the office network, firewall, VPN tunnel, and cloud systems, plus a complete written firewall rule set including the fix for the identified connectivity gap.

slots.practicalActivity: Continue the capstone build: write the verification test you'd run to prove the fix actually worked (a specific ping, curl, or traceroute command against the inventory system's real or placeholder address, with the expected successful result stated). Then draft the README section for this project: the brief, the requirements, and the design decisions (why this CIDR, why DHCP plus static reservations, why a VPN instead of exposing the office to the internet).
slots.deliverable: A written verification test (command plus expected result) proving the connectivity fix worked, plus a drafted README covering the brief, requirements, and design decisions.

slots.practicalActivity: Assemble the finished capstone portfolio entry: combine your architecture diagram, README, and verification test from the last two sessions with a 4-sentence problem/fix narrative following the lesson's exact shape (what broke, how you isolated it, what you found, how you fixed it). Then write out, in your own words, how you'd present this project out loud in an interview in under 60 seconds.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone portfolio packet (architecture diagram, README, verification test, and a 4-sentence problem/fix narrative), plus a written 60-second spoken walkthrough of the project for an interview.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can read an IP address and subnet correctly, explain how a packet actually gets from a laptop to a cloud server across DNS/TCP/HTTP/TLS, configure basic firewall and VPN access, and run a real bottom-up diagnosis with ping/traceroute/dig/curl/ss when something stops working — the ground-floor networking and cloud literacy every later DevOps course assumes.
